"'''Black Museum'''" is the sixth and final episode of the fourth season of anthology series ''[[Black Mirror]]''. It was directed by [[Colm McCarthy (director)|Colm McCarthy]] and written by series creator [[Charlie Brooker]], with one part adapted from a story by [[Penn Jillette]]. The episode premiered on [[Netflix]], along with the rest of series four, on 29 December 2017. The episode is divided into three stories, told by Rolo Haynes ([[Douglas Hodge]]), the owner of a remote Black Museum. He tells the visitor Nish ([[Letitia Wright]]) about the backstories of various exhibits, which involve his previous employment in experimental technologies.

"Black Museum" was filmed over a month in Spain and [[Nevada]], United States. A [[horror (genre)|horror]] episode, its themes include race and technology. The set contained a large number of [[Easter egg (media)|Easter eggs]] referencing previous works in the series. "Black Museum" was met with mixed critical reception: most reviewers found its storyline and characterisation poor and the final plot twist proved polarising. The episode generally received weak rankings by critics in comparison to other ''Black Mirror'' episodes. Wright received a [[Primetime Emmy Award]] nomination and a [[Black Reel Award]] nomination for her acting.

==Plot==
Nish ([[Letitia Wright]]) is driving across the desert, presumably in the [[United States]]. While waiting for her car to charge, she visits the remote Black Museum. The proprietor, Rolo Haynes ([[Douglas Hodge]]), explains backstories to the museum's crime-related arte<!-- Correct British English spelling; do not change -->facts, starting with a hairnet device.

Rolo previously recruited people for experimental medical technology. In a flashback, Dr. Peter Dawson ([[Daniel Lapaine]]) agreed to test an implant that made him feel the physical sensations of the person wearing the hairnet, to help him diagnose patients quickly. After experiencing a man's death, he became aroused by his patients' pain. Developing a [[sadomasochism|masochistic]] addiction to it, he started mutilating himself for pleasure and eventually murdered a homeless man after forcing the hairnet on him, which caused him to fall into a coma.

In the present, the air conditioner is broken, so Nish offers Rolo water. Moving on to a toy monkey, Rolo describes how he convinced Jack ([[Aldis Hodge]]) to transfer his comatose wife Carrie's ([[Alexandra Roach]]) consciousness into part of his brain, so she could experience his physical sensations and communicate with him. Jack and Carrie became aggravated by their lack of privacy and [[agency (philosophy)|agency]], respectively. Rolo offered Jack an ability to "pause" Carrie. Months later, Jack un-paused her, and they eventually agreed for her to be un-paused on weekends only. Jack began dating Emily (Yasha Jackson), who wanted Carrie to be deleted. Rolo transferred Carrie to the toy monkey, which could feel sensations and say two phrases ("Monkey loves you" and "Monkey needs a hug"). Carrie and Jack's son Parker was soon bored by it. The monkey technology became illegal due to the limited emotions available, so Rolo was fired.

The museum's centerpiece is a holographic Clayton Leigh ([[Babs Olusanmokun]]). Rolo insists he was guilty of murder but Nish reminds him of conflicting evidence. While on [[death row]], Clayton signed up to Rolo's exhibit: when a visitor pulls a lever, a conscious hologram of Clayton receives the [[electric chair]], and a souvenir copy of him experiencing electrocution is made. The exhibit was immensely popular. As Rolo begins to have difficulty breathing, Nish continues the story, revealing herself as Clayton's daughter. After public protests, attendance to the exhibit dwindled to sadists and wealthy white supremacists, who abused Clayton's consciousness so heavily he was left in a [[vegetative state]]. Nish's mother Angelica ([[Amanda Warren]]) overdosed the day after she saw him. As revenge, Nish sabotaged the air conditioner and gave Rolo poisoned water. Nish transfers Rolo's consciousness into Clayton's hologram, then electrocutes it, which creates a souvenir of Rolo's suffering.

Nish takes the monkey containing Carrie with her and sets the museum on fire. She converses with her mother, whose consciousness is inside her head, like Carrie's was with Jack. She hangs the Rolo souvenir on her car's rear-view mirror, and drives away from the museum as it burns down.

===Conception and writing===
[[File:Penn Jillette by Gage Skidmore.jpg|thumb|right|upright|The first story in this episode was based on the short story "The Pain Addict", written by [[Penn Jillette]] in the 1980s.]]
The episode is a combination of three stories, the same structure as the 2014 special "[[White Christmas (Black Mirror)|White Christmas]]". Brooker described it as a narrative of "punishment and racism", similar to series two episode "[[White Bear (Black Mirror)|White Bear]]", and with a tone resembling the 1990s American horror anthology series ''[[Tales from the Crypt (TV series)|Tales from the Crypt]]''. Some of the ideas used in "Black Museum" had been discussed prior to the production of series four. Brooker had conceived earlier of a [[ghost story]] involving a digital prisoner who was repeatedly electrocuted. Other ideas from this time included people having other consciousnesses implanted in their brain, such as a person who had an ex-partner in their brain, or a person who rented out parts of their brain to dead people.<ref name="ibm"/>

The first part of the anthology, involving Dr. Peter Dawson, was based on the short story "The Pain Addict" authored by magician [[Penn Jillette]] early in his career.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://heavy.com/entertainment/2017/12/penn-jilette-pain-addict-black-mirror-museum-buy/ | title = 'Black Mirror': All About Penn Jillette's Pain Addict | first = Stephanie Dube | last = Dwilson | date = 29 December 2017 | access-date = 1 January 2018 | work = [[Heavy.com]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180102073222/http://heavy.com/entertainment/2017/12/penn-jilette-pain-addict-black-mirror-museum-buy/ | archive-date = 2 January 2018 | url-status = live }}</ref> Jillette had written the story based on the personal experience of being ill in a Spanish welfare hospital in 1981, where it was difficult to get a diagnosis due to the language barrier. He conceived of technology that allowed a doctor to understand what pain a person was suffering, but led to the doctor's addiction to the pain of others. The story continued with the doctor "beating people to feel their pain", engaging in [[sadomasochism]] and desiring to experience what [[Jesus]] felt while being crucified.<ref name="slashfilm jillette"/> The idea was published as a short story in the 1988 anthology ''Would, Could, Should''.<ref>{{cite tweet|last=Jillette|first=Penn|author-link=Penn Jillette|user=pennjillette|number=950591803207573505|date=8 January 2018|title=Wow.  I had forgotten it was published there.  Wow.|access-date=11 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Derrickson|first=Fraser|date=1988|title=Would, Could, Should: The Science Fiction Society Anthology}}</ref> Jillette met with Brooker before the production of the third series and told him about the story.<ref name="slashfilm jillette"/>

Around two years later, Brooker contacted Jillette to explain that he wanted to use "The Pain Addict" as a story in "Black Museum". Jillette then worked with Brooker on the framing story, which would involve a washed-up Las Vegas [[carny]] running the Black Museum outside of Vegas. Jillette wanted to audition for the role of the carny, but the production was too far along to change the casting.<ref name="slashfilm jillette">{{cite web | url = https://www.slashfilm.com/black-mirror-season-4-penn-jillette/ | title = 'Black Mirror' Season 4 Will Feature a Story Conceived by Penn Jillette | first = Jacob | last = Hill | date = 22 May 2017 | access-date = 1 January 2018 | work = [[/Film]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171229130002/http://www.slashfilm.com/black-mirror-season-4-penn-jillette/ | archive-date = 29 December 2017 | url-status = live }}</ref> Brooker took Jillette's past performances as part of Penn & Teller and his documentary series ''[[Penn & Teller: Bullshit!|Bullshit!]]'' as inspiration for Rolo.<ref name="ibm">{{cite book | title=  Inside Black Mirror | date = November 2018 | first1 = Charlie | last1 = Brooker | first2 = Annabel | last2 = Jones | first3 = Jason | last3 = Arnopp | chapter = Black Museum | isbn = 9781984823489 | publisher =  [[Crown Publishing Group]] | place = New York City }}</ref>

===Casting and filming===
The production had previously looked to cast Letitia Wright in an episode of the third series of ''Black Mirror'', but she became unavailable. During casting for "Black Museum", Wright was at the end of shooting for the superhero film ''[[Black Panther (film)|Black Panther]]'', where she worked with the star of the first series episode "[[Fifteen Million Merits]]", [[Daniel Kaluuya]]. She provided a self-tape audition, with Kaluuya reading the other characters' lines. Filming took place immediately after ''Black Panther''{{'}}s filming ended.<ref name="ibm"/>

Douglas Hodge starred in the episode as Rolo Haynes, describing his character as a [[white supremacist]] and "the most toxic person" he had played. Hodge stayed largely in character during the filming process, staying away from Wright and choosing not to rehearse lines off-screen.<ref name="ibm"/> Daniel Lapaine appears in this episode as Dr. Peter Dawson, after playing an unrelated role in the series one episode "[[The Entire History of You]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://heavy.com/entertainment/2017/12/black-museum-cast-characters-black-mirror/|title=Black Museum: Meet the Cast from the Black Mirror Episode|work=[[Heavy.com|Heavy]]|last=Dwilson|first=Stephanie Dube|date=29 December 2017|access-date=31 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171231103500/http://heavy.com/entertainment/2017/12/black-museum-cast-characters-black-mirror/|archive-date=31 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Colm McCarthy (director)|Colm McCarthy]] directed the episode. It took a month to film, with locations including Spain and [[Nevada]], United States.<ref name="variety production"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://onset-hollywood.com/black-mirror-black-museum-2017-filming-locations-netflix-original-series/|title=Black Mirror: Black Museum (2017) Filming Locations – Netflix Original Series|website=OnSetHollywood.com|access-date=24 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180212033141/http://onset-hollywood.com/black-mirror-black-museum-2017-filming-locations-netflix-original-series/|archive-date=12 February 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Hodge's scenes were shot in chronological order. During the first story, Rolo shows Dr. Dawson a pair of rats, for which stuffed frozen rats were used. The first story also featured a graphic sex scene, which took a long time to film relative to its brief screentime. Scenes which relate to the plot twist of Nish's true intentions at the museum—such as her first sighting of the museum, her handing Rolo water and her entering the exhibit where her father is—were shot in many different ways. Wright played the early scenes as if Nish was the tourist she claims to be.<ref name="ibm"/>

===Post-production===
Brooker and executive producer [[Annabel Jones]] participated in the edit of the episode, aiming to find a more human side to Rolo's character at certain points, and omitting some of the darker moments.<ref name="ibm"/>

The music for the episode was composed by [[Cristobal Tapia de Veer]], who commented on the score: "The beginning, discovering the Black Museum, that was going to set the tone for the rest of the show. The music morphed in many ways throughout the three stories, then goes back to where it started with the Black Museum, although with a sense of accomplishment, but also a sense of doom."<ref>{{cite web|last1=Barkan|first1=Jonathan|title=Exclusive: Venture Into Black Mirror's Black Museum with Cristobal Tapia de Veer's We Got a Miracle|url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/264999/exclusive-venture-black-mirrors-black-museum-cristobal-tapia-de-veers-got-miracle/|website=Dead Central|date=19 January 2018|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403162339/https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/264999/exclusive-venture-black-mirrors-black-museum-cristobal-tapia-de-veers-got-miracle/|archive-date=3 April 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Sophie Gilbert]] of ''[[The Atlantic]]'' found that the episode's structure was very similar to the previous portmanteau instalment "White Christmas".<ref name="atlantic">{{cite news|last1=Gilbert|first1=Sophie|title='Black Mirror': 'Black Museum' Is a Throwback to Episodes Past|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2017/12/black-mirror-black-museum-is-a-throwback-to-episodes-past/549389/|access-date=14 June 2020|work=[[The Atlantic]]|date=31 December June 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> "Black Museum" has a linear narrative and Jacob Oller of ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' believed that the three stories are "darker and darker" as they progress.<ref name="wired"/><ref name="paste">{{cite web|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-review-black-museum/|title=In the Superb "Black Museum," Black Mirror Looks at Its Own Reflection|work=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]|last=Oller|first=Jacob|date=3 January 2018|access-date=14 June 2020}}</ref> Tasha Robinson of ''[[The Verge]]'' commented that it explores the genre of "traditional horror".<ref name="wired"/><ref name="verge">{{cite web|last1=Robinson|first1=Tasha|title=In Black Museum, Black Mirror finally finds a single person to blame for technology|url=https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/3/16845504/black-mirror-black-museum-review-netflix-season-4-douglas-hodge-letitia-wright|website=[[The Verge]]|access-date=24 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180124135822/https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/3/16845504/black-mirror-black-museum-review-netflix-season-4-douglas-hodge-letitia-wright|archive-date=24 January 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> Louise Mellor of ''[[Den of Geek]]'' found it the "most cynical episode of the season".<ref name="dog">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-4-black-museum-review/|title=Black Mirror season 4: Black Museum review|last=Mellor|first=Louise|work=[[Den of Geek]]|date=29 December 2017|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200518171408/https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-4-black-museum-review/|archive-date=18 May is dangerous", it revolves around Rolo being "personally loathsome".<ref name="verge"/> Mellor commented that the first story is "physically horrid", the second "wickedly cruel" and the third a "sad story" with "no laughs".<ref name="dog"/> Reviewing the stories' tones, Robinson found the first to be "dim and claustrophobic", the second "naturalistic" and the last "shot with a [[exploitation film|grind house]] seediness".<ref name="verge"/>

The episode was compared by Robinson to the 1990s horror anthology series ''Tales from the Crypt'', with Rolo Haynes in a role similar to the cryptkeeper.<ref name="verge"/> Christopher Hooton of 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200404180146/https://www.vulture.com/2017/12/black-mirror-recap-season-4-black-museum.html|archive-date=4 April 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Gabriel Tate of ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'' found the consciousness transfer into a person's brain to be similar to the comic strip series ''[[The Numskulls]]'', where small beings maintain the characters' brains and bodies.<ref name="tele">{{cite news|last1=Tate|first1=Gabriel|title=Black Mirror, season 4, Black Museum, review: a treasure trove of Easter Eggs and perfunctory shocks|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-season-4-black-museum-review-treasure-trove-easter/|access-date=14 June 2020|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|date=29 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620142115/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-season-4-black-museum-review-treasure-trove-easter/|archive-date=20 June 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Mellor found the use of "[[(There's) Always Something There to Remind Me]]" in the ending to be a punchline characteristic of ''Black Mirror''{{'}}s fourth series.<ref name="dog"/>

Rolo Haynes is a "stand-in narrator", according to Steve Green of ''[[IndieWire]]''.<ref name="indie">{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2017/12/black-mirror-black-museum-review-ending-series-spoilers-1201911893|title='Black Mirror': 'Black Museum' is the Kind of Season Finale a Show Makes When It's Ready to End|work=[[IndieWire]]|last=Greene|first=Steve|date=30 December 2017|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200509052455/https://www.indiewire.com/2017/12/black-mirror-black-museum-review-ending-series-spoilers-1201911893/|archive-date=9 May 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Bramesco called him a "storyteller" with a role similar to Matt Trent in "White Christmas".<ref name="vulture"/> Jason Parham of ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' found him to be "an opportunistic sociopath" like the 19th century circus owner [[P. T. Barnum]].<ref name="wired">{{cite magazine|first=Jason|last=Parham|title=Why ''Black Mirror''{{'}}s Most Controversial New Episode Is Its Most Important|url=https://www.wired.com/story/black-mirror-black-museum/|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|date=1 June 2018|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200305080532/https://www.wired.com/story/black-mirror-black-museum/|archive-date=5 March 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Noel Ransome called Rolo "a figure of the white and the western, who senselessly use the black and the misguided for personal gain".<ref name="vice">{{cite news|title=I'm a Black Critic Who Dismissed the 'Black Museum' Episode|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/im-a-black-critic-who-dismissed-the-black-museum-episode/|access-date=14 June 2020|work=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]]|last=Ransome|first=Noel|date=5 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190810094404/https://www.vice.com/en_ca/article/59w53k/im-a-black-critic-who-dismissed-the-black-museum-episode|archive-date=10 August 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> The ending saw Rolo the victim of the technology he had created, similar to Robert Daly's outcome in series four episode "[[USS Callister]]".<ref name="vulture"/> Convicted murderer Clayton Leigh's innocence was disputed by critics,<ref name="vox"/> Zack Handlen of ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' finding him innocent but Tate believing it to be ambiguous.<ref name="tele"/><ref name="avclub">{{cite news|last1=Handlen|first1=Zack|title=''Black Mirror'' ends its fourth season with a dud|url=https://www.avclub.com/black-mirror-ends-its-fourth-season-with-a-dud-1821635228|access-date=14 June 2020|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|date=29 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191225131308/https://www.avclub.com/black-mirror-ends-its-fourth-season-with-a-dud-1821635228|archive-date=25 December 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> Ransome wrote that he serves as "the standard black man", who "begins with enthusiasm and ends with exhaustion".<ref name="vice"/> The ending can be interpreted as happy, with Rolo getting what he deserved.<ref name="avclub"/> Bramesco found that the programme "doesn't condemn" Nish, only the "ugly racism" of Rolo.<ref name="vulture"/> Parham found the story to be about "cruelty of the prison system" and saw Nish freeing her father as a symbolic act.<ref name="wired"/> Greene called Nish's actions "an act of mercy" to Clayton.<ref name="indie"/>

The episode includes [[Easter egg (media)|Easter egg]] references to each of the 18 previous ''Black Mirror'' episodes, according to McCarthy; many were placed by set designer Joel Collins.<ref name="variety production"/> Gilbert said that this "seemed to definitively tie the ''Black Mirror'' universe together".<ref name="atlantic"/> Collins said that he wanted to make the set a "hidden celebration of six years of ''Black Mirror''".<ref name="ibm"/> For example, Jack is seen reading a comic showing plot points from "Fifteen Million Merits", and the museum's entrance includes a screen showing a picture of [[Victoria Skillane]], a mannequin with a black balaclava and a white two-pronged symbol—all from "White Bear". The two rats shown to Dawson by Haynes are named Kenny and Hector, referencing the main characters from "[[Shut Up and Dance (Black Mirror)|Shut Up and Dance]]". The episode also makes multiple allusions to "[[San Junipero]]", including the company TCKR, a hospital named Saint Juniper's and Yorkie and Kelly's dresses being on display in the museum.<ref name="variety production">{{cite web | url = https://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-black-museum-colm-mccarthy-directing-interview-1202640505/ | title = 'Black Mirror' Director on 'Black Museum': 'I Think There's Something Quite Spiritual About It' | first = Danielle | last = Turchiano | date = 29 December 2017 | access-date = 1 January 2018 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180111102248/http://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-black-museum-colm-mccarthy-directing-interview-1202640505/ | archive-date = 11 January 2018 | url-status = live }}</ref><ref name="heavy">{{Cite web |url=http://heavy.com/entertainment/2017/12/black-museum-easter-eggs-photos-screenshots-mirror/ |title=Black Museum Easter Eggs: Photos of Every Black Mirror Episode Mentioned [SPOILERS] |last=Dwilson |first=Stephanie Dube |date=29 December 2017 |website=Heavy.com |access-date=31 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171229122344/http://heavy.com/entertainment/2017/12/black-museum-easter-eggs-photos-screenshots-mirror/ |archive-date=29 December 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The term "Black Museum" was the original name for the [[Crime Museum]], a museum of crime arte<!--this is the proper spelling for British English - do not change-->facts at [[Scotland Yard]] in the United Kingdom.<ref name="atlantic"/> Greene believed the museum served as an analogy to the series, which is about "finding addictive entertainment value in the plight of removed dystopias".<ref name="indie"/> Many museum items are taken from previous episodes, for instance: an autonomous drone insect (ADI) from "[[Hated in the Nation]]"; the lollipop Daly uses to clone Walton's son in "USS Callister"; the tablet used by Marie in "[[Arkangel (Black Mirror)|Arkangel]]"; and the bloodied bathtub where Shazia's husband was murdered in "[[Crocodile (Black Mirror)|Crocodile]]".<ref name="variety production"/><ref name="heavy"/> Separately, one wall of the museum includes a number of [[death mask]]s, which are busts of crew members.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-reveals-hang-dj-inspiration-1074803 | title = 'Black Mirror': Charlie Brooker Reveals Inspiration for "Hang the DJ" | first = Jackie | last = Strause | date = 15 January 2018 | access-date = 16 January 2018 | work = [[The Hollywood Reporter]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180115231423/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-reveals-hang-dj-inspiration-1074803 | archive-date = 15 January 2018 | url-status = live }}</ref>

==Reception==
[[File:Letitia Wright by Gage Skidmore.jpg|upright|right|thumb|[[Letitia Wright]] received a [[Primetime Emmy Award]] nomination for her performance.]]
"Black Museum" received a mixed critical reception.<ref name="vice"/> On review aggregator [[Rotten Tomatoes]], it has an approval rating of 75%, based on 28 reviews. The website's critics consensus reads: "''Black Mirror'' goes full ''Black Mirror'' in 'Black Museum', an anthology within the anthology that has hits, misses, and plenty of philosophical sinew to chew on."<ref name="RottenTomatoes">{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s04/e06|title=Black Museum|publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190411195946/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s04/e06|archive-date=11 April 2019|url-status=live}}</ref> It received ratings of three out of five stars in ''The Telegraph'', a C+ in ''The A.V. Club'' and a C− in ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''.<ref name="tele"/><ref name="avclub"/><ref name="ew"/> Sonia Saraiya of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' called it the "worst episode" of the series, Darren Franich of ''Entertainment Weekly'' finding it the "only outright stinker".<ref name="ew">{{cite magazine|title=Black Mirror's new season boldly riffs on Star Trek and online dating: EW review|url=https://ew.com/tv/2017/12/06/black-mirror-review/|access-date=14 June 2020|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|date=6 December 2017|last=Franich|first=Darren|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200325203100/https://ew.com/tv/2017/12/06/black-mirror-review/|archive-date=25 March 2020|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="variety">{{cite news|last1=Saraiya|first1=Sonia|title=TV Review: 'Black Mirror' Season 4 on Netflix|url=https://variety.com/2017/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-tv-review-1202648385/|access-date=14 June 2020|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=23 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203154600/https://variety.com/2017/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-tv-review-1202648385/|archive-date=3 February 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Handlen reviewed that its "obvious setups" led to the work lacking "surprise or insight", while Tate found that the characters were not developed well.<ref name="tele"/><ref name="avclub"/> Robinson reviewed that despite themes of punitive justice and racism, the commentary was "too vague".<ref name="verge"/> Contrastingly, Ransome found it the "most satisfying" instalment of the series, commenting that many reviewers "all seemed blind to the episode's overarching thesis on race".<ref name="vice"/> Hooton opined that it was "very strong".<ref name="independent"/>

Franich criticised that the episode's three stories are only "vaguely connected", Caroline Framke of ''[[Vox (website)|Vox]]'' finding that "none particularly stand out".<ref name="vox">{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2017/12/29/16822796/black-mirror-black-museum-recap-season-4-review|title=Black Mirror's "Black Museum" tour tells 3 stories of pain and forced symbiosis|work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|last=Framke|first=Caroline|date=29 December 2017|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180124043030/https://www.vox.com/culture/2017/12/29/16822796/black-mirror-black-museum-recap-season-4-review|archive-date=24 January 2018|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="ew"/> Saraiya believed that the narrative requires "people repeatedly choosing to be stupid and/or evil".<ref name="variety"/> Handlen called the stories "mean-spirited".<ref name="avclub"/> However, Hooton called the stories "engrossing".<ref name="independent"/> Tate found the first to be "competent if predictable", though Gilbert reviewed that the homeless man's murder was "one of the most gratuitously violent scenes" in the show.<ref name="atlantic"/><ref name="tele"/> Tate found the second story the best, though Framke thought it "not especially convincing" and Bramesco believing Jack to be the "dumbest man in history" for agreeing to the consciousness transfer into his head.<ref name="vulture"/><ref name="tele"/><ref name="vox"/>

The final story and ending received mixed reception. Bramesco found that it "doesn't make a whole lot of sense in terms of storytelling" and Rebecca Nicholson of ''[[The Guardian]]'' thought it repeated previous themes of the series.<ref name="vulture"/><ref name="guardian">{{cite news|last1=Nicholson|first1=Rebecca|title=Black Mirror review: the Netflix series is back – and darker than ever|url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2017/dec/29/black-mirror-review-netflix-series-back-darker-charlie-brooker|access-date=14 June 2020|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=29 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171229125055/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2017/dec/29/black-mirror-review-netflix-series-back-darker-charlie-brooker|archive-date=29 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> Gilbert said it "isn't exactly a satisfying conclusion"; on the other hand, Framke called it "incredibly satisfying".<ref name="atlantic"/><ref name="vox"/> Mellor found the twist to be "great" and "satisfying", though Tate thought only the reveal that Nish's mother's consciousness was inside her head was "genuinely unexpected".<ref name="dog"/><ref name="tele"/> Framke called the third story overall "deeply cruel and entirely believable".<ref name="vox"/> Mellor commented that the ending was "happy" and "optimistic" and sees "justice done".<ref name="dog"/>

McCarthy's role as director was praised by Tate, who said that he "directs with imagination throughout".<ref name="tele"/> Oller approved of the episode's "clever visual effects" and use of props.<ref name="paste"/> The acting received mixed reception, Tate calling them "serviceable although seldom spectacular."<ref name="tele"/> Mellor found that Wright and Hodge offered "two excellent performances", with Gilbert finding Wright the "most compelling".<ref name="atlantic"/><ref name="dog"/> Oller thought that the dialogue was "clunky" in places.<ref name="paste"/>

===Episode rankings===
"Black Museum" received largely poor rankings on critics' lists of the 23 instalments of ''Black Mirror'', from best to worst:
{{col-begin}}
{{col-2}}
* 9th – Travis Clark, ''[[Business Insider]]''<ref name="insider ranking">{{cite web|url=http://businessinsider.com/every-black-mirror-episode-on-netflix-ranked-from-worst-to-best-2018-5|title=All 23 episodes of Netflix's 'Black Mirror,' ranked from worst to best|work=[[Business Insider]]|last=Clark|first=Travis|date=10 September 2018|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180911115114/https://www.businessinsider.com/every-black-mirror-episode-on-netflix-ranked-from-worst-to-best-2018-5|archive-date=11 September 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 13th – Matt Donnelly and Tim Molloy, ''[[TheWrap]]''<ref name="wrap ranking">{{cite web | url=https://www.thewrap.com/all-19-black-mirror-episodes-ranked-from-good-to-mind-blowing-photos/ | title='Striking Vipers' to 'National Anthem': Every 'Black Mirror' Ranked, From Good to Mind-Blowing (Photos) | author=Donnelly, Matt | author2=Molloy, Tim | website=[[TheWrap]] | access-date=14 June 2020 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180217192830/https://www.thewrap.com/all-19-black-mirror-episodes-ranked-from-good-to-mind-blowing-photos/ | archive-date=17 February 2018 | df=dmy-all }}</ref>
* 17th – Charles Bramesco, ''Vulture''<ref name="vulture ranking">{{cite web | url=http://www.vulture.com/2016/10/every-black-mirror-episode-from-worst-to-best.html | title=Every ''Black Mirror'' Episode, Ranked | author=Bramesco, Charles | date=21 October 2016 | website=[[Vulture.com|Vulture]] | access-date=14 June 2020 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180312082859/http://www.vulture.com/2016/10/every-black-mirror-episode-from-worst-to-best.html | archive-date=12 March 2018 | df=dmy-all }}</ref>
* 18th – Aubrey Page, ''[[Collider (website)|Collider]]''<ref name="collider ranking">{{cite web | url=https://collider.com/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/ | title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked From Worst to Best | date=28 October 2016 | last=Page | first=Aubrey | work=[[Collider (website)|Collider]] | access-date=14 June 2020 | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202134910/http://collider.com/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/ | archive-date=2 February 2018 | df=dmy-all }}</ref>
{{col-2}}
* 20th – Corey Atad, ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]''<ref name="esquire ranking">{{cite web | url=http://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a49919/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/ | title=Every Episode of ''Black Mirror'', Ranked | date=24 October 2016 | author=Atad, Corey | website=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] | access-date=14 June 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815171949/http://www.esquire.com/entertainment/tv/a49919/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/ | archive-date=15 August 2017 | url-status=live}}</ref>
* 20th – Morgan Jeffery, ''[[Digital Spy]]''<ref name="ds ranking">{{cite web|url=http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/feature/a780434/black-mirror-episodes-ranked-charlie-brooker/|title=Ranking all 23 episodes of Charlie Brooker's chilling Black Mirror|website=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Jeffery|first=Morgan|date=9 April 2017|access-date=14 June 2020|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180806110935/http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/feature/a780434/black-mirror-episodes-ranked-charlie-brooker/|archive-date=6 August 2018}}</ref>
* 21st – [[James Hibberd (writer)|James Hibberd]], ''Entertainment Weekly''<ref name="ew ranking">{{cite magazine | url=https://ew.com/gallery/black-mirror-episodes-ranked/?slide=283289#283289 | title=Every ''Black Mirror'' Episode Ranked (including season 5) | author=Hibberd, James | author-link=James Hibberd (writer) | date=23 October 2016 | magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] | access-date=14 June 2020 | df=dmy-all }}</ref>
* 23rd – Ed Power, ''The Telegraph''<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-every-episode-ranked-rated/|title=Black Mirror: every episode ranked and rated, from Striking Vipers to San Junipero|newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|last=Power|first=Ed|date=28 December 2017|access-date=14 June 2020|url-access=limited|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101030556/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-every-episode-ranked-rated/|archive-date=1 January 2018}}</ref>
{{col-end}}

Instead of by quality, Proma Khosla of [[Mashable]] ranked the episodes by tone, concluding that "Black Museum" is the 7th-most pessimistic episode of the show.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread|title=Every 'Black Mirror' episode ever, ranked by overall dread|publisher=[[Mashable]]|last=Khosla|first=Proma|date=5 January 2018|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180308090919/https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread/|archive-date=8 March 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>
